title: Fit Maps Overview In Clo 2026.0

markdown_content: ## Fit Maps Overview (CLO 2026.0) This section introduces how Fit Maps help compare garment fit across different fabrics and explain what the four Fit Maps (stress, strain, fit, pressure) are used for. It also frames the demo: two identical garments on the same avatar, differing only by fabric type (knit vs pleather/leather-like). In the example, the speaker uses **CLO** with **two garments that are identical** on the **same avatar** (same size and avatar). The only difference is the fabric: one is **knitted**, the other is a **leathery pleather**-type material. The goal is to use **Fit Maps** to see how each fabric changes the resulting fit, stress, strain, and pressure on the avatar. Fit Maps are located in the **3D toggle menu**, directly **under the fabric icon**, using the **Fit Map icon**. There are **four fit maps** available: - **Stress** - **Strain** - **Fit** - **Pressure** You **cannot view them all at once**; you must open them **individually**. Hovering over the icon also reveals shortcuts to each map. --- ## Pre-Fit Setup Checklist (Avatar, Garment, Simulation) This section covers the required preconditions for accurate Fit Map results: pattern piece resolution (particle distance), skin offset, and using the correct simulation mode (**Fitting**). These settings ensure pressure/strain readouts are meaningful. Before using Fit Maps, confirm these items are set correctly in CLO: ### 1) Pattern pieces: particle distance - Ensure **pattern pieces are at least 5** in **particle distance**. - The speaker notes that **5** provides clearer detail for fitting, revealing folds/scrunching more accurately. - (They mention **20** is great for editing, but **5** is preferred for fitting detail.) Example workflow: - Select a **pattern piece** - Check **particle distance** (target **5**) - Verify under the **Property Editor** ### 2) Skin offset: set to zero - Ensure **skin offset is at least 1** in the checklist sense, but the speaker’s preferred/required value is effectively: - **skin offset = 0** (they state “zero is better” and “should be at zero”) - In the property editor, they reference related values such as: - **static friction = 0.8** - **kinetic friction = 0.05** - **skin inward offset = 5** - They emphasize that the most important one for Fit Maps accuracy is **skin offset**. Why it matters: - **Skin offset = 0** means the garment sits **directly on top of the avatar**. - This removes “pretend air” spacing that exists during editing. - The speaker explains this is critical because Fit Maps (especially pressure/strain) need accurate contact to measure **how much the garment is pushing on the avatar**. ### 3) Simulation mode: use **Fitting**, not Normal - Set **simulation to “Fitting”** (they specifically say **do not** use **Normal**). - **Fitting sim** produces more accurate results, but takes more time. - GPU fitting is allowed if available; otherwise, on Mac it uses **CPU**. - The speaker emphasizes: **edit** on other modes if needed, but **fit** using **Fitting sim**. --- ## Fit Map Tools: Custom View and Tape Tools This section documents usability features that help interpret Fit Maps: using **Custom View** for consistent camera angles and using **tape tools** to check alignment to specific avatar areas. ### Custom View (personal preference) The speaker prefers: - Right-click → **Custom view** - Choose an angle/view they’re used to - Reset view when needed after moving/zooming This helps ensure they’re still evaluating fit correctly. ### Tape tools (alignment checks) If you need to ensure a garment hits a specific line or position: - Use the **tape tools** to draw tape on the avatar - This helps verify whether the garment alignment matches expectations --- ## Stress Map (KPA): Force Per Unit Area This section explains what the **Stress** Fit Map measures, how to interpret its numeric/color scale, and clarifies directionality (pressure on fabric vs pressure on body). ### What Stress Map displays The speaker uses the definition: - **Displays the force per unit area in KPA applied to a garment by external stress** - Interpreted as: how much **pressure is in the fabric per section** due to a **tight fitted garment** Important clarification: - Stress/pressure readings relate to **how much the body/skin applies to the garment**, not how the fabric would push back (the speaker frames it as “pressure the fabric is putting on your body” vs “pressure your body is putting on the fabric,” emphasizing you must understand what the map is measuring). - They stress that the **fabric pressure** is the key concept: it reflects the pressure resulting from the garment fit/contact. ### Interpreting colors and global values The Stress Map includes: - A **gradient color scale** - chunks.title: Fit Maps Overview In Clo 2026.0
chunks.content: ## Fit Maps Overview (CLO 2026.0) This section introduces how Fit Maps help compare garment fit across different fabrics and explain what the four Fit Maps (stress, strain, fit, pressure) are used for. It also frames the demo: two identical garments on the same avatar, differing only by fabric type (knit vs pleather/leather-like). In the example, the speaker uses **CLO** with **two garments that are identical** on the **same avatar** (same size and avatar). The only difference is the fabric: one is **knitted**, the other is a **leathery pleather**-type material. The goal is to use **Fit Maps** to see how each fabric changes the resulting fit, stress, strain, and pressure on the avatar. Fit Maps are located in the **3D toggle menu**, directly **under the fabric icon**, using the **Fit Map icon**. There are **four fit maps** available: - **Stress** - **Strain** - **Fit** - **Pressure** You **cannot view them all at once**; you must open them **individually**. Hovering over the icon also reveals shortcuts to each map. --- ## Pre-Fit Setup Checklist (Avatar, Garment, Simulation) This section covers the required preconditions for accurate Fit Map results: pattern piece resolution (particle distance), skin offset, and using the correct simulation mode (**Fitting**). These settings ensure pressure/strain readouts are meaningful. Before using Fit Maps, confirm these items are set correctly in CLO: ### 1) Pattern pieces: particle distance - Ensure **pattern pieces are at least 5** in **particle distance**. - The speaker notes that **5** provides clearer detail for fitting, revealing folds/scrunching more accurately. - (They mention **20** is great for editing, but **5** is preferred for fitting detail.) Example workflow: - Select a **pattern piece** - Check **particle distance** (target **5**) - Verify under the **Property Editor** ### 2) Skin offset: set to zero - Ensure **skin offset is at least 1** in the checklist sense, but the speaker’s preferred/required value is effectively: - **skin offset = 0** (they state “zero is better” and “should be at zero”) - In the property editor, they reference related values such as: - **static friction = 0.8** - **kinetic friction = 0.05** - **skin inward offset = 5** - They emphasize that the most important one for Fit Maps accuracy is **skin offset**. Why it matters: - **Skin offset = 0** means the garment sits **directly on top of the avatar**. - This removes “pretend air” spacing that exists during editing. - The speaker explains this is critical because Fit Maps (especially pressure/strain) need accurate contact to measure **how much the garment is pushing on the avatar**. ### 3) Simulation mode: use **Fitting**, not Normal - Set **simulation to “Fitting”** (they specifically say **do not** use **Normal**). - **Fitting sim** produces more accurate results, but takes more time. - GPU fitting is allowed if available; otherwise, on Mac it uses **CPU**. - The speaker emphasizes: **edit** on other modes if needed, but **fit** using **Fitting sim**.
